title: Creation
lead: The Bible opens and closes with creation: God made the heavens and the earth (Genesis 1–2), keeps them in being (Psalm 104; Colossians 1:17), and will make them new (Isaiah 65:17; Revelation 21:1). Creation is praised in psalms, argued in Job and the prophets, and tied to Christ in John 1 and Colossians 1.

sections.b:
Genesis 1 tells creation as an ordered week of God's commands; Genesis 2 as a potter shaping a man and planting a garden. The poets tell it again in other ways: God stretches out the heavens like a tent and sets the earth on its foundations (Psalm 104:2–5), shuts in the sea with doors (Job 38:8–11), and makes the world by wisdom (Proverbs 8:22–31). Isaiah calls on the Creator as Israel's guarantee in exile (Isaiah 40:26–28; 45:18). The New Testament adds that all things were made through the Word (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2), that creation shows God's power (Romans 1:20), and that it waits for its own freedom (Romans 8:19–22).

The idea of creation from nothing first appears clearly in 2 Maccabees 7:28 (in the Catholic and Orthodox canon; compare Hebrews 11:3) and became standard Jewish and Christian teaching, though scholars debate whether Genesis 1 itself teaches it or describes God ordering a dark, watery world (Jon Levenson, John Walton), and when the technical doctrine took shape (Gerhard May dates it to the second century AD). How Genesis 1 relates to modern science is discussed under The Days of Creation.
